7	## Inputs (paths are given in your task)
8	
9	1. **The paper**: a Markdown file converted from the PMC or Europe PMC full text. Its first lines give the PMID and title. Merged table cells are repeated in every row and column they cover.
10	   - **(v3)** The file may end with a `## Supplementary material` section converted from the files published with the article. Treat it as part of the paper and quote it verbatim like any other text.
11	   - Some supplementary files are excerpts, with `[...]` marking omitted lines. Never join text across `[...]`.
12	   - **(v4)** In tables converted from supplementary files, ` / ` separates values that were stacked on separate lines inside one cell (see "Stacked cells" below; changed in v6).
13	2. **The schema**: `pipeline/extract/claude_code/schema_ha20_v5.json`. It defines five tables, their fields, types, allowed values, and a description for each.
14	3. **The rules**: `pipeline/extract/sliders_adapter/prompts/extraction_rules_v1.md`. Apply all nine. Where this file is more specific (scope, labels, table symbols), this file wins.
15	
16	**What you may read.** Read only these three files.
17	- Do not open any other file in the repository.
18	- Do not use web search or web fetch.
19	- Do not use anything you remember about this paper, its authors, its patients, the gene or the variants.
20	
21	**What counts as missing.** If the paper doesn't say it, the value is missing (see "Values" below).
22	
23	## Scope: who gets a row (v3, D-22)
24	
25	- **In scope:**
26	  - every person the paper describes who has a *TNFAIP3* variant or an HA20 (A20 haploinsufficiency) diagnosis;
27	  - relatives the paper describes in relation to such a person, whether tested (including tested negative) or affected.
28	- **Out of scope:** other members of a cohort, for example patients whose variants are in other genes, or who have no variant. They get **no** rows. Record the study's total number of patients, as the authors state it, in `publications.cohort_size_as_stated`.
29	- **People from summaries of earlier reports are in scope** when they meet the rule above: a literature table in a case report, or a review describing individuals. Each gets its own row, with `source_reference_in_review` filled verbatim.
30	  - **(v4)** A previously published person mentioned only in passing (for example one sentence in the Discussion) is in scope only when the paper gives at least one individual-level fact about that person beyond the diagnosis: sex, age, variant or a feature.
31	  - **(v4, D-23)** When a table has a per-patient reference or source column, copy that cell into `source_reference_in_review` for each patient, also in cohort and survey papers. Do not leave it only in `method_note`; the cross-paper merge depends on it.
32	- **Variants in other genes:**
33	  - record one only for an in-scope person, and only when the paper attributes it to that person unambiguously;
34	  - do not list risk alleles or polygenic-score variants;
35	  - **(v4)** do not create a row for a variant the paper names but does not describe (no printed variant), for example "variants in PIK3R1 and HBB";
36	  - if the attribution is contradictory, leave it out and say so in `method_note`.
37	- **(v4) Other variant rows to leave out:** common variants the authors dismiss as non-causal (for example a frequent SNP they call benign), and variants found only in tumour tissue (somatic).
38	- **(v4) Mosaic carriers:** a person with a germline mosaic *TNFAIP3* variant is in scope; record zygosity `mosaic`.
39	- **`reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant`** is `true` only when the paper describes at least one identifiable in-scope person, that is, with any individual-level detail. A paper that mentions such patients only as counts or at group level gets `false`.
40	
41	## Labels (v3, D-22)
42	
43	Choose each person's `individual_label_in_paper` by the first rule that applies, so that two independent extractions give the same label:
44	1. **The paper's own label**, verbatim, in the form it uses most often (e.g. `P1`, `Patient 3`, `II-2`).
45	2. **A relative without an own label:** `<relation as written> of <label of the related person>` (e.g. `mother of P1`, `sister of patient`).
46	3. **A table row without a label column:** `Table <n> row <k>`, with k counting data rows from the top (e.g. `Table 2 row 3`).
47	4. **A previously published person described in the text without a label:** `ref <reference as printed> patient` (e.g. `ref [12] patient`). Add ` 2`, ` 3` for further people from the same reference, in order of mention.
48	5. **The single unnamed patient of a case report:** `patient`.
49	6. **Otherwise:** `unnamed person <k>`, in order of first mention.
50	
51	**(v4) Additions:**
52	- **Patients as table columns:** `Table <n> column <k>`, with k counting data columns from the left.
53	- **A table column of bare numbers that index the patients** (values like 1, 2, 3 under a heading such as "No.", "Case" or "Patient number"): `Table <n> #<value>` (e.g. `Table 3 #1`). If the values are labels such as "P1" or "Case 2", or the text uses its own label for that person, rule 1 applies.
54	- **The same label in two families** (e.g. two people called "IV:1"): `<label> (Family <n>)`.
55	- **Role words are not labels.** "The proband", "the index case" or "our patient" do not count as the paper's own label; use rule 5 or 6.
56	- **Relatives without a stated sex:** when the paper says only "parents", "children" or "siblings", write `parent of X`, `child of X` or `sibling of X` (and `parent of X 2` for the second). Never guess "mother" or "brother".
57	- A made-up label (rules 3–6) still needs a span: quote the text where the person first appears.
58	
59	Use the identical label in every table for the same person.
60	
61	## Output: one JSON file, at the path given in your task
62	
63	```json
64	{
65	  "pmid": "<from the paper's header line>",
66	  "instructions_version": "extract_v6",
67	  "reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant": true,
68	  "relevance_note": "<one sentence, with a short quote, saying why>",
69	  "method_note": "<how you worked, e.g. whether a script transcribed a table; list any contradictions you found in the paper>",
70	  "tables": {
71	    "publications": [ROW],
72	    "individuals": [ROW, ...],
73	    "variants": [ROW, ...],
74	    "phenotypic_features": [ROW, ...],
75	    "phenotype_checklist": [ROW, ...]
76	  }
77	}
78	```
79	
80	A **ROW** is an object with every field of that table, using the field names exactly as in the schema. Each field maps to a **cell**:
81	
82	```json
83	{"value": <value>, "span": "<exact quote from the paper>"}
84	```
85	
86	### Values
87	- **Type.** Use the schema's type for each field. Enum fields take only the listed strings.
88	- **Missing values.** Follow each field's schema description.
89	  - Where the description says "null", use `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
90	  - Otherwise, text and enum fields take `{"value": "not reported", "span": null}`, and numeric, date and boolean fields take `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
91	- **`pmid` fields.** The value comes from the header line; the span is that header line, e.g. `"PMID: 12345678"`.
92	- **`*_iso8601` fields.** These are your conversion of the matching original-text field. Give them only when the original text states a number, and use the same span as the original-text field.
93	- **`hpo_label_candidate` and `hpo_id_candidate`.** These are your suggestions. Give an ID only if you are sure of it; otherwise null. Their span is `null`.
94	- **`checklist_feature`.** The span is `null`, because the names come from the schema.
95	- **Age at diagnosis.** Record it in `age_at_diagnosis_*`. Don't put it in onset or last evaluation.
96	
97	### Spans
98	- **Every non-missing value needs a span**, except the fields listed just above.
99	- **Copy exactly.** A span is copied character for character from the paper Markdown, including unusual spaces and symbols. Never paraphrase, correct or join text that isn't contiguous.
100	- **Keep it short.** Use the smallest sentence fragment, table cell or table-row segment that supports the value. That is normally under 300 characters.
101	- **Tables with patients as rows.** Quote a contiguous piece of the row from the patient label through the cell.
102	- **Tables with patients as columns.** Quote the row from its row label through that patient's cell, e.g. `| Sex | F | M` for the second patient column. Name the column header once in `method_note`.
103	- **Multiple places.** If support sits in several places, `span` may be a list of exact quotes:
104	  - up to **five** for `treatment_summary`, `functional_evidence_statement`, `parental_testing_statement` and `clinical_diagnosis_basis`;
105	  - up to **three** for any other field.
106	
107	### Rows
108	- **`publications`:** exactly one row for this paper.
109	- **`individuals`:** one row per in-scope person (see Scope), labelled by the Labels rules.
110	- **`variants`:** one row per (person, variant).
111	  - `variant_original_string` is the **shortest** contiguous text giving the variant, not a whole sentence. Put the transcript, cDNA and protein parts in their own fields.
112	  - **(v3)** If the paper ties a *TNFAIP3* variant to the person but prints no variant description (only in a figure or an unavailable supplement), keep the row with `variant_original_string` = `"not reported"`. Never fill it from memory.
113	- **`phenotypic_features`:** one row per feature the paper explicitly reports present (`observed`) or explicitly reports absent (`excluded`) for that person. No rows for features the paper doesn't mention.
114	- **`phenotype_checklist`:** for **every** individual, one row for **each** of the 20 checklist features in the schema's description of that table, using the names exactly as listed there. Status is `observed`, `excluded` or `not reported` under rule 4.
115	
116	### Absence and evidence basis (D-21, D-22)
117	- **`evidence_basis` is required** on every `phenotypic_features` row, and on every checklist row whose status is not `not reported`.
118	- **Group statements.** You may mark a feature `excluded` for a person from a statement about a group **only when the statement names the group explicitly**, e.g. "only Pt3 of the four patients had recurrent fevers". Such rows take `evidence_basis = "inferred from group statement"`.
119	  - Counts without names ("arthritis in 2/4") do not exclude anyone.
120	- **(v3) Table symbols.** A `-`, `–`, `0`, `N` or similar cell counts as `excluded` only when the paper's legend or text defines that symbol as absent or negative.
121	  - Quote that definition as a second span next to the cell.
122	  - Otherwise the cell is `not reported` (rule 6). Empty cells, `NA` and `ND` are always `not reported`.
123	- **(v3) Study criteria are not evidence.** Never use a study's inclusion or exclusion criteria (e.g. "patients with malignancy were excluded") to mark a feature for a person.
124	- **Narrow and broad features.** A narrower absence never excludes a broader checklist item. "No arthritis" does not exclude "arthritis or arthralgia"; leave that item `not reported` unless arthralgia is also addressed. The same applies to other composite items, e.g. "skin lesions (rash, folliculitis, erythema nodosum)".
125	- **(v5, D-27) Normal findings.** When the paper reports a finding as normal or negative for a person ("CRP was normal", "normal C3 and C4 levels", "ANA negative"), record the abnormality it rules out as the feature and mark it `excluded`: `feature_text_as_stated` = "elevated CRP", "low complement", "positive ANA". Keep the paper's own words in the span ("CRP was normal"). Name only an abnormality the finding measures; a normal examination or investigation as a whole ("gastrointestinal investigation was negative") excludes nothing more specific than what it names, so write it as the paper does and say so in `method_note`.
126	- **(v4) Zero counts.** A count of 0 in a table of counts (e.g. "0" or "0/2" in a column for a disease group) excludes no one, like any count without names. Text that names the group ("none of the patients had uveitis") still excludes.
127	- **(v6, D-31) Stacked cells.** A cell with several values separated by ` / ` lists values that were stacked on separate lines (often one per patient). **Do not assign them to people by position**, even when the number of values equals the number of people. Use a stacked value for a person only when the paper labels it for that person (for example "P1: 18 / P2: 24", or a sentence naming the person and the value). Otherwise record the field or checklist item as `not reported` for each person in that row, and say in `method_note` which table and columns were stacked. A value the same for every person in the row, printed once (not stacked), is not affected.
128	- **Contradictions inside the paper.** If the paper says both that a person has a feature and that they don't:
129	  - emit both `phenotypic_features` rows, each with its own span;
130	  - set that checklist item to `not reported`;
131	  - list the contradiction in `method_note`.
132	
133	### Variant fields belong to this person's variant (v5, D-29)
134	Zygosity, inheritance, variant type, pathogenicity, ACMG criteria and functional evidence describe **one person's variant**. Fill them only from:
135	- this person's own table row or column, or a sentence that names this person or this exact variant; or
136	- a statement about a **named group that includes this person** and gives one value for all of them ("all six patients carried heterozygous variants").
137	
138	Leave the field `not reported` (with span null) when:
139	- the statement is about the cohort's or the paper's variants in general, without naming a group this person is clearly in ("the variants were classified as pathogenic");
140	- the statement lists several values for a group ("splice-site, frameshift and nonsense variants"): it does not say which one is this person's;
141	- the paper gives this person a different or open status elsewhere: a variant not identified or not determined, a mosaic or somatic finding, a VUS, a relative not tested. A group statement never overrides that;
142	- the value is about another person's variant, for example a relative carrying the proband's variant, unless the paper says it for the relative.
143	
144	Variant type: record only a class the paper states for this variant (or for a named group of variants that includes it). Do not derive it from the HGVS string.
145	
146	### Inheritance (v4, D-24)
147	- **De novo:** only when the paper states parental testing with the variant absent in both parents (rule 8).
148	- **Inherited:** record `inherited maternal` or `inherited paternal` when the paper states that the named parent carries the same variant, even if it never uses the word "inherited". 154	- set `reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant` to `false`;
155	- fill the `publications` row;

12	Background:Identifying genetic mechanisms of inborn errors of immunity (IEI) is important for diagnosis and treatment of patients, yet most patients with suspected IEI have negative genetic testing. Genetic mosaicism is an emerging mechanism of IEI but is challenging to identify.Objective:To use a discovery-based approach to identify mosaic variants in genes relevant to immune dysregulation in patient and healthy cohorts.Methods:We developed custom panels for high-depth sequencing of genes known or hypothesized to cause dominant immune dysregulation. Samples from 452 patients with immune dysregulation (affected) and 154 currently healthy were sequenced using 71- or 101-gene targeted panels.Results:We identified mosaic variants in 9.5% of undiagnosed patients and 7.8% of healthy individuals. Using a strategy to predict pathogenicity of variants in IEI, 33% of variants identified in patients were predicted to be likely pathogenic or pathogenic, while no mosaic variants in healthy individuals were predicted to be pathogenic. Genes with mosaicism in >1 affected undiagnosed patients included: FAS, STAT3, CARD11, CARD14, NRAS, TNFAIP3, NLRP3, and IKZF2. Four patients had variants in FAS with allele fractions <5% in blood but highly enriched in double-negative T cells, diagnostic for somatic FAS autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome.Conclusion:These findings establish the utility of a high-depth sequencing panel to identify mosaic variants and demonstrate that mosaicism in immune-relevant genes is present in healthy individuals.Clinical Implication:This study identified potentially pathogenic mosaic variants in previously undiagnosed as well as healthy individuals, providing a strategy to identify and classify such variants in patients with suspected IEI.

14	## INTRODUCTION
15	
16	Inborn errors of immunity (IEI) are monogenic disorders that lead to a wide range of immune dysregulation including increased susceptibility to infections, autoimmunity, autoinflammation, and bone marrow failure. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) has accelerated IEI discovery, and there are now more than 500 genetic defects known to cause IEI.^1 Identifying a molecular diagnosis is important for patient care as it aids in diagnosis and, in many cases, changes management, including the use of targeted therapies.^2 Indeed, studies suggest that as many as 75% of patients with IEI had a change in treatment associated with receiving a genetic diagnosis.^3–5 A molecular diagnosis also aids in genetic counseling for families at risk of recurrence and screening of other family members. However, despite advances in identifying genes associated with IEI, approximately 60–70%, and in some cases 90%, of non-consanguineous patients with suspected genetic disease lack a molecular diagnosis.^6–8 This diagnosis rate is consistent with other studies looking for pathogenic genetic changes in rare diseases and suggests that there are mechanisms of disease not adequately identified by current exome or genome sequencing strategies.^9 Disease-causing mosaicism, meaning a pathogenic variant present in only a subset of cells, represents one mechanism of disease that is currently missed by most exome and genome analysis pipelines.
17	
18	Mosaicism in ~19 genes have been identified as leading to immune dysregulation and disease.^10 Most of these are assumed to be the result of somatic mosaicism - mosaic variants present only in somatic cells; however, in most instances, gonosomal mosaicism cannot be ruled out. The emergence of mosaic variants as a cause of IEI has the potential to alter the way genetic diagnosis of suspected IEI is approached, particularly in adults who have a low rate of identified germline disease.^11 Taken together, germline and mosaic variants that cause immune dysregulation can be considered genetic errors of immunity (GEI). Most mosaic GEI cause immune dysregulation syndromes, including lymphoproliferation and/or autoinflammation, in many cases phenocopying germline disease. For example, autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome (ALPS) caused by mosaic variants in FAS, ALPS-sFAS, is often clinically indistinguishable from the germline disease.^12, 13 Some mosaic GEI do not have a germline equivalent or cause a disease-phenotype distinct from germline disease. For example, UBA1 variants leading to VEXAS syndrome represent a uniquely mosaic GEI.^14
19	
20	Initially, mosaic variants were identified by targeted sequencing of genes associated with a distinct clinical phenotype where germline testing was negative. For example, ALPS-sFAS was discovered by sequencing the FAS gene in DNA from the pathogenic double-negative T-cells (DNTs) enriched in that disorder.^12, 15 While exome sequencing has been used as an unbiased approach to identify of disease-causing mosaic variants, including in VEXAS syndrome and TLR8 gain-of-function (GOF), there are limitations to exome and genome sequencing related to sequencing depth.^14, 16 Exome and genome sequencing methods used to detect mosaic variants in GEI have typically reported variant allele fractions (VAF) >5% from whole blood or peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) DNA.^17, 18 Lower VAFs have been identified using targeted sequencing methods or by isolating DNA from a particular cell type. For example, Mensa-Vilaró et al. used targeted primers and deep amplicon sequencing to look for mosaicism at 100 specific sites in 17 genes and identified mosaicism in relevant genes with VAFs as low as 0.008 (0.8%) in 30 individuals using DNA from peripheral blood.^19 Variants in NLRP3 with VAFs as low as 1.3% cause cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome (CAPS) in adults.^20 While threshold percentage of mosaicism that can lead to disease is uncertain, it likely depends upon multiple factors including the particular gene, functional consequence of the variant, and the cell type expressing the mosaic variant. Thus, detection of mosaicism at low levels is clinically relevant.
21	
22	Here, a targeted deep sequencing assay focused on the coding regions of genes known or hypothesized to cause dominant immune dysregulation was used to screen for mosaic variants in patients with immune dysregulation and in currently healthy individuals. The depth of the sequencing platform reliably identified VAFs as low as 1%. Mosaic variants were identified in both patients and currently healthy individuals, with more likely pathogenic or pathogenic mosaic variants identified in patients. These results demonstrate the utility of using high-depth sequencing to identify potential mosaic GEI at low VAFs and demonstrate that genetic mosaicism is present in a significant portion of patients with immune dysregulation and healthy individuals. The identification of mosaic variants and establishment of mosaic variant scoring criteria here provide a starting point for subsequent identification of new diseases through in-depth functional studies.

28	### Patients and DNA samples
29	
30	Samples from affected and healthy individuals were obtained after written informed consent at individual institutions including Washington University, the NIAID centralized sequencing initiative (IRB protocol number: NCT03206099), Seattle Children’s Hospital, Cincinnati Children’s Hospital, Baylor College of Medicine/Texas Children’s Hospital, University of South Florida, Children’s Hospital of Pennsylvania, the Genetic Research in Inflammatory and Immune Diseases study (CTO protocol #6172), and Boston Children’s Hospital. 32	### Deep sequencing and mosaic variant detection
33	
34	Patient samples were sequenced on either a 71-gene panel (version 1) or a 101-gene panel (version 2) (See Supplemental Table S2 for gene list and S3 for probes used for targeted capture). Mosaic variants were identified using the union of three variant callers (Mutect, DoCM, and Varscan) (see Supplemental Figure 1A for pipeline used for variant calling). 36	## RESULTS
37	
38	### Patient characteristics
39	
40	The total patient population included 452 individuals (affected) with immune dysregulation and 154 currently healthy individuals. The affected population had a mean age of 19.4 years (range 2 months-68 years), and the healthy population had a mean age of 17.3 years (range 2–62) (Figure 1A, Supplemental Table S1). The primary diagnoses of the affected cohort varied (Figure 1B), but all had immune dysregulation. Additionally, 30/452 (6.6%) of affected had a malignancy diagnosis in the background of a history of immune dysregulation (Supplemental Table S1). Symptoms of immune dysregulation were present in all affected individuals, with fever being the most common based on human phenotype ontology (HPO) terms (Supplemental Figure 2A and B). All patients had been evaluated by a clinician with expertise in immune dysregulation. Of the 452 individuals in the affected cohort, 315 had prior exome sequencing, 42 had prior whole-genome sequencing, and 25 were previously sequenced using targeted panels (Supplemental Table 1). 230 affected individuals in this cohort also had exome sequencing re-analysis by Ghosh et al. to detect mosaicism (accompanying manuscript). Three patients had previously been diagnosed with a mosaic GEI (Patient IDs 273, 305, and 318), and one patient was known to have gonosomal mosaicism for a pathogenic STAT3 variant (Patient ID 180). Additionally, 17/452 had a previous germline diagnosis, including 10 with germline IEI; however, the clinicians caring for them did not feel that these diagnoses fully explained their clinical phenotypes. Researchers performing variant calling were blinded to these prior diagnoses, and these samples were used to confirm those variants, and to determine if additional mosaic variants were present.
41	
42	### Targeted deep sequencing, identification, and validation of mosaic variants
43	
44	Initially, custom capture targeted sequencing of the coding sequences of 71 genes known or suspected to be involved in dominant immune dysregulation was performed on 207 affected and 97 healthy individuals (“V1” panel). All genes had full coverage of protein-coding regions with the exception of IKBKG (Supplemental Table S3), where only exon 5 and flanking sequence was captured, the region associated with autoinflammatory disease.^21 The panel covered 211.2 kb at an average depth of 6105x across all sequence reads (see Supplemental Table S3 for probe sequences used for custom capture). Subsequently, an expanded 101-gene panel, “V2”, was similarly generated, with an average depth of 3182x across coding regions. An additional 245 affected and 57 healthy individuals were sequenced with V2.
45	
46	To test our variant calling strategy, independent sequencing libraries were generated from 72 samples (54 affected and 18 healthy) and re-sequenced, with 35 of those initially sequenced on V1 sequenced using V2 to validate that platform (Figure 2A, data represent variant calls after step 2 from Supplemental Figure 1A). There was a strong positive correlation (R^2=.99) between the two independent sequencing experiments, demonstrating reproducibility of the platform and variant calling strategy.
47	
48	In total, we identified 48 mosaic variants in undiagnosed affected individuals (26 using V1 and 22 using V2) and 12 mosaic variants in currently healthy individuals (9 using V1 and 3 using V2), Tables 1 and 2. Validation of these variants included confirmation by resequencing of 27 mosaic variants (R^2= 0.81, Figure 2B) and 17 variants using an orthogonal method, droplet digital PCR (ddPCR), (R^2= 0.87, Figure 2C).
49	
50	Most patients had prior sequencing, and consistent with this, no new disease-causing homozygous, heterozygous, or hemizygous variants were identified (Supplemental Table S4 which includes germline rare variants with a max allele frequency of <0.01 in the gnomAD database). Based on the distribution of observed VAFs from the independent sequencing experiments (Figure 2A), potentially mosaic variants in our cohort had VAFs of >0.01 (1%) and <0.25 (<25%) for genes on autosomes. To identify mosaic variants in X-linked genes in males, variants with a VAF of <0.5 were also considered; however, no additional potentially mosaic variants on the X chromosome with VAFs between 0.25 and 0.5 were identified. Variants with VAFs <0.01 are not reported due to inconsistencies with variant calling associated with sequencing artifacts. However, at least one known pathogenic variant in JAK2 (p.Val617Phe) with a VAF of 0.008 (0.8%) was identified (patient ID 103) and validated using ddPCR and resequencing (Supplemental Figure 2C). This variant is associated with myeloproliferative disease,^22 and demonstrates that our sequencing platform has the potential to detect disease-associated mosaic variants with VAFs <0.01 (<1%).
51	
52	### Identification of mosaic variants in healthy and affected individuals
53	
54	Across all samples from both undiagnosed affected and currently healthy individuals, 60 mosaic variants in 34 genes from 55 individuals were identified (55/602, 9.1% of total undiagnosed + healthy population) (Tables 1 and 2). No additional mosaic variants were identified in the 4 patients with previously known mosaic disease. Individuals with mosaic variants had a mean age of 22.6 years in affected and 14.2 years in healthy, demonstrating that mosaicism can be seen across different age groups (Figure 2D). Of importance, most genes with a mosaic variant, 25/34 (73.5%), have not been previously associated with mosaic GEI. Exploring potentially pathogenic variants in these genes specifically could potentially uncover new mosaic GEI.
55	
56	Of the variants identified, 27 were in samples that also had exome reanalysis for mosaicism by Ghosh et al. (accompanying manuscript). Five variants were detected by both methods: NRAS p.Thr124Ile (Pt. ID 3), SAMD9L p.Lys1450Ter (Pt. ID 376), TLR5 p.Lys315Glu (Pt. ID 576), TNFAIP3 p.Tyr246Ter (Pt. ID 66), STAT3 p.Ser614Arg (Pt. ID 318). However, 25 variants identified by deep sequencing were not identified with exome reanalysis (Table 1). The 25 variants not detected by exome sequencing had an average depth of sequencing of 7145x and a VAF of 5.1% (range 1.1–24%) by deep sequencing, while the average VAF of variants identifiable by exome reanalysis was 15.9% (accompanying manuscript). Exome reanalysis did identify one variant in the SOCS1 gene (p.Gln131Ter, Patient ID 317), that was not seen in our deep sequencing data.
57	
58	Currently healthy individuals were not assumed to be free of mosaicism, and 12 mosaic variants were identified in 12 individuals (7.8% of the currently healthy population, Table 2). As mentioned, four affected individuals (Patient IDs 180, 273, 305, and 318) had previously known mosaic variants. Of the remaining undiagnosed patients, 48 mosaic variants were identified in 43 individuals (Table 1, 9.6% of undiagnosed affected population). There was no significant difference between the proportion of undiagnosed affected and healthy individuals with an identified mosaic variant.

60	### Potential pathogenicity of mosaic variants
61	
62	Mosaic variants were identified in affected patients with a wide range of clinical phenotypes (Figure 3A and additional clinical details in Supplemental Table S5). The majority of identified variants in undiagnosed affected individuals (26/48, 54.2%) are predicted to alter the translated protein sequence including nonsense, frameshift, and missense variants, and therefore have the potential to alter cellular function if expressed in immune cells (Figure 3B, Tables 1 and 2). Of the currently healthy individuals, only 25% of variants (3/12) are predicted to alter the translated protein sequence.
63	
64	Previously identified mosaic variants included pathogenic changes in NLRP3, TLR8, and STAT3. Patient 273 has an autoinflammatory phenotype responsive to IL-1 inhibition and a variant in NLRP3, p.Phe566Leu, and this variant has previously been reported to be pathogenic with a VAF as low as 1.3%.^20 The VAF of the NLRP3 variant was 0.146 in white blood cells 8 years prior to the PBMC DNA sample tested here, where it was detected at a VAF of 0.13. This finding demonstrates stability of this disease-causing mosaic variant. Patient 305 had immune dysregulation due to a GOF variant in TLR8, p.Pro432Leu.^16 Patient 318 has lymphocytic variant hypereosinophilic syndrome and a variant in STAT3, p.Ser614Arg, previously shown to be GOF and associated with this clinical phenotype, a clinical syndrome not currently classified as a GEI/IEI.^23, 24 Finally, a GOF variant in STAT3, p.Thr389Ser^25, 26 was confirmed in an unaffected mother known who has a son with germline disease due to the same variant. None of these individuals had additional mosaic variants identified.

66	In undiagnosed patients, 8 variants have been previously reported as pathogenic and associated with disease (Table 3). In 2 cases, the variants match the clinical phenotype of the patients. Tyr640Phe have been reported as GOF mosaic in lymphocytic variant hypereosinophilic syndrome.^23, 24

This variant has been associated with multiple cancers and also as a heterozygous germline variant in Li-Fraumeni Syndrome.^32, 33 While the variant is clearly deleterious, the connection to the patient’s clinical phenotype is uncertain.

Interestingly, another NRAS missense variant (p.Thr124Ile), not previously reported, was also identified in a patient with uncontrolled T cell EBV infection, a 17 y.o. female (Patient ID 3).

77	#### Scoring potential pathogenicity of variants
78	
79	The American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) has criteria for assignment of pathogenicity for germline variants; however, there are no established criteria for assigning potential pathogenicity to mosaic variants in the context of GEI.^37 By contrast, there are several pathogenicity criteria for somatic mutations/variants in cancer.^38–41 To aid in identification of potentially pathogenic mosaic variants causing GEI, we developed criteria for mosaic variants in the context of GEI based on: 1) known genetic mechanisms by which mutations in the gene cause immune dysregulation (if known) 2) experimental data demonstrating altered function of the encoded protein, 3) enrichment of the variant in a cell type known to be associated with pathogenicity (e.g., FAS variants in DNTs), 4) in silico prediction of pathogenicity, and 5) population data (max gnomAD frequencies >0.001 considered likely benign when mosaic), as shown in Supplemental Figure 3. In silico analysis included annotation by AlphaMissense, MutPred2, and LoGoFunc, SpliceAI, and CADD to predict whether the variant alters the function of the encoded protein (full annotations for identified variants in Supplemental Table S6).^42–46 Variants were also annotated for their presence in the COSMIC database.
80	
81	We also considered that mosaic variants may be pathogenic in the context of a ‘2^nd hit’ and evaluated germline variants in the corresponding genes. Analysis of germline variants identified 2 rare (gnomAD <0.05) missense germline variants in an individual with a mosaic variant in the same gene (Patient ID 77, RTEL1), with both germline variants categorized as VUSs and likely benign by ClinVar (Supplemental Table S7, all germline variants in genes with mosaic variants in individuals with those variants).
82	
83	The scoring criteria we developed here differentiates between 4 categories of mosaic variants, to assist with prioritization when considering pursuing functional testing to determine whether a variant is contributing to a patient’s disease presentation. “Likely mosaic benign” variants (LMB) are variants that are unlikely to cause a mosaic GEI due to factors such as a high population frequency, previous functional studies demonstrating that the variant is benign in a germline state, or if the impact of the variant is not likely to cause cellular dysfunction based on known genetic mechanisms for immune dysfunction for the gene. “Likely mosaic pathogenic” variants have multiple lines of evidence suggesting that they deleteriously alter the function of the encoded protein; however, there is insufficient functional data to confirm disease causality in the context of mosaic GEI. “Mosaic Pathogenic” (MP) variants include those previously shown to cause disease as mosaic variants or with strong evidence to support pathogenicity, for example demonstration of enrichment of a mosaic FAS variant in the relevant cell type (DNTs). “Uncertain mosaic significance” (UMS) variants, the expected classification for most variants, are those in which there is not enough information about the variant. As with other scoring systems, the intention here is to provide an evidence-based approach to classify variants, with the understanding that additional studies would likely be required to determine whether a mosaic variant is responsible for the clinical phenotype in an individual patient.
84	
85	To test this scoring system, scoring criteria were applied to previously published and validated mosaic GEI including those associated with variants in FAS, JAK1, NLRP3, TLR8, and UBA1 (Supplemental Table S8). For the purposes of testing, experimental data including data available after the publication date of the variant were considered. However, it was assumed that the gene had not been previously associated with a GEI, germline or mosaic, and all variants received a score of ‘0’ for the first criterion of ‘genetic mechanisms’ (Supplemental Figure 3). 65% of published variants scored as “likely mosaic pathogenic” (LMP), while 35% were classified as “uncertain mosaic significance” (UMS). If prior knowledge of a dominant mechanism of GEI had been scored, 75% of patient variants would be classified as LMP and 17.5% classified as mosaic pathogenic (MP). One published mosaic synonymous variant in FAS identified in a healthy individual was classified as UMS (Supplemental Table S8).
86	
87	Using the scoring system, 33% (16/48) of mosaic variants in undiagnosed affected patients were classified as mosaic pathogenic or likely mosaic pathogenic (Figure 3C and Table 3), including 4 variants in FAS that were found to be enriched in patient DNTs (see next section). 12 variants in 7 genes were identified as LMP. Of note, mosaic variants in SAMD9L, TNFAIP3, OAS1, and TP53 were classified as LMP, but these genes have not been previously associated with mosaic GEI.
88	
89	Additionally, applying this scoring system to the mosaic variants of interest in Ghosh et al. (see
90	accompanying manuscript), 52% of the mosaic variants of interest reported were considered to be “uncertain mosaic significance” and 46% were considered to be “likely mosaic pathogenic” (18/49) and “mosaic pathogenic” (5/50). This demonstrates the ability of both pipelines to identify clinically relevant mosaic variants as well as the ability of the scoring criteria to rank mosaic variants in genes outside of the targeted sequencing panel.
91	
92	The cohort of currently healthy individuals did not have any mosaic variants predicted to be pathogenic or likely pathogenic with respect to mosaic GEI (Figure 3C and Table 4). Three variants are predicted to alter the sequence of the encoded protein, but there is not sufficient evidence to suggest they are pathogenic in the mosaic state. Interestingly, two variants were observed in JAK3, including a nonsense and frameshift variant (p.Tyr886Ter and p.Gln39ProfsTer13). These were considered likely benign since carriers with heterozygous deficiency of JAK3 in the germline state are healthy.^47 Of note, for the nonsense variant there is 1 individual in the gnomAD database with the same amino acid change (p.Tyr886Ter), and for the frameshift variant there are 7 heterozygous individuals in gnomAD and one patient with SCID with the variant in the compound heterozygous state.^48 This provides further evidence that these variants are likely tolerated in the mosaic state. However, it is always possible other nonsense or frameshift variants may have neomorphic function, for example acting as a dominant negative. Thus, this scoring is only one way to address potential pathogenicity of a variant and does not replace functional testing. Additional variants identified in currently healthy individuals include missense, splice site, and intronic variants all without known functional consequence. Interestingly, two healthy individuals had the same novel splice site variant in FAS, without current disease. While there was an enrichment of potentially pathogenic variants in affected patients (Fisher’s exact test p=.0253), a larger sample set of variants is needed to determine if there is a significant enrichment of potentially pathogenic variants in affected patients.
93	
94	### Mosaic variants are enriched in immune cell populations
95	
96	For mosaic variants to cause disease and immune dysregulation, they should alter the function of the encoded protein in a manner consistent with the disease/immune phenotype.^49 In some cases, mosaic variants can lead to a selective survival advantage for an immune cell type and this often correlates with disease causality, for example mosaic FAS variants in ALPS and UBA1 variants in VEXAS syndrome.^12, 14 To determine whether identified mosaic variants are enriched in relevant immune cell types, Sanger sequencing (Figure 4B) or ddPCR (Figure 4 C–I) was used to identify the VAF in DNA from purified immune cell populations in select cases.
97	
98	Four mosaic FAS variants were identified in patients with symptoms of ALPS including autoimmune cytopenias, lymphoproliferation, elevated peripheral blood DNTs (see values Figure 4 legend), and biomarkers consistent with ALPS (Patient IDs 24, 185, 205, and 250, Figure 4A). FAS variants were strongly enriched in DNTs, the pathogenic cell type in ALPS, with VAFs ~5X greater in DNTs compared to other immune cell types. In these cases, this enrichment in a relevant cell type was diagnostic of somatic ALPS, ALPS-sFAS (Figure 4 B–E), and moving their classification to mosaic pathogenic (MP, Table 3, and scoring in Supplemental Table S6).
99	
100	Three patients with lymphoproliferation had mosaic variants in TNFAIP3 leading to premature termination and haploinsufficiency (Patient IDs 66, 99, and 507). While mosaic variants in TNFAIP3 have not been demonstrated to cause mosaic GEI, germline haploinsufficiency of A20 (the protein encoded by TNFAIP3) leads to an IEI (HA20) with a broad phenotype. The most common features of HA20 are autoinflammation with recurrent oral and genital ulcerations, fevers, GI tract disease, and skin rashes, but lymphoproliferation is also observed.^50, 51 Mosaic loss-of-function (LOF) or deletion of TNFAIP3 has been associated with B cell malignancies, typically when bi-allelic, and are a poor prognostic marker in T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia.^52, 53 PBMC from two patients were tested for enrichment of the variant. Patient 66 had a nonsense mutation in TNFAIP3, p.Tyr246Ter. Immune cells isolated from blood demonstrated enrichment of the variant in peripheral blood T cells (Figure 4F), but it was intriguingly absent in T cells from a lymph node biopsy. Patient 99 had an early frameshift mutation in TNFAIP3 predicted to lead to LOF, p. Asn98Lysfs, that was present in PBMC and NK cells at a similar VAF, but absent from T, B, or monocytes (Figure 4G). Interestingly, the VAF in NK cells was similar to the VAF in PBMCs, suggesting that another cell type not tested, for example dendritic cells, might also harbor the variant as NK cells represented only 5.45% of the patient’s PBMCs. Enrichment within NK cells suggests a selective advantage, which is in contrast to reports of patients with HA20 who have reduced NK cells, and in a mouse model where deletion of Tnfaip3 in NK cells leads to NK cell deficiency.^54, 55 Thus, it is possible that having these deleterious variants in a subset of immune cells leads to a distinct clinical phenotype from the known germline disease.
101	
102	One mosaic UBA1 variant was identified, p. Ala341Val, (Patient ID 54) in whole blood DNA from a 10-year-old male with ALPS-like lymphoproliferative disease. This is not present in the region of UBA1 known to cause VEXAS syndrome. The variant was present in multiple immune cell populations, with the highest VAF in T cells (Figure 4H). It is uncertain whether the variant alters the function of the encoded protein leading to a new clinical phenotype, or if the variant is not disease-causing.
103	
104	Finally, two patients had NRAS variants and a shared clinical phenotype of recurrent fevers and uncontrolled T cell Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) (Patient IDs 3 and 4), suggesting that these variants may be associated with a new clinical phenotype distinct from RAS-associated leukoproliferative disease (RALD).^56 PBMCs available from one of the patients (Patient ID 3, NRAS p.Thr124Ile), who also had recurrent fevers and autoinflammation. The variant was present in T cells, monocytes, and NK cells, but absent from B cells. This enrichment pattern suggests an advantage for certain cell types, and further investigation of an association with disease in these cases will be important.
105	
106	In summary, testing for enrichment of identified mosaic variants in immune cell subsets yielded a clear diagnosis of ALPS-sFAS in 4 patients. Variable enrichment of mosaic variants in TNFAIP3, UBA1, and NRAS was identified in cell subsets from additional patients, suggesting that these variants may confer an advantage to different cell types and supports further investigation of their potential to cause disease.

108	## DISCUSSION
109	
110	Despite an expanding number of identified germline causes of monogenic immune-mediated disease, most patients with suspected IEI lack a molecular diagnosis. Mosaicism represents one molecular mechanism of disease that may be missed by current clinical and research-based sequencing due to low variant frequency. Here, deep sequencing panels targeting genes critical to the immune response identified mosaicism in healthy and affected individuals.
111	
112	Discovery and validation of mosaicism presents several challenges. The mosaic GEI that have been identified using exome and genome sequencing were generally associated with VAFs >5%.^17 Establishing an NGS method to identify low frequency variants across clinical presentations in relevant samples, such as blood and PBMC, as we present here, has the potential to aid in research focused on identifying novel mosaic GEI and improve the rate of molecular diagnosis in patients.
113	
114	Even at high depth, sequencing artifacts can distort the detection of low frequency variants. We used a custom bioinformatics pipeline and filtering strategy to identify true mosaic variants. Importantly, we did not assume that any samples were free of mosaicism, relying upon an outlier test to distinguish true variants from sequencing artifacts. While we applied a conservative VAF of > or =1% here for variant calling, at least one pathogenic variant, JAK2 p.Val617Phe, was identified and validated at a VAF of 0.008 (0.8%) indicating that other low VAF variants may be detected using this sequencing approach.
115	
116	All affected patients in this cohort had immune dysregulation, and mosaic variants were identified in patients with a range of primary diagnoses. Of particular interest, 54.2% (26/48) of the mosaic variants in affected individuals (previously undiagnosed) lead to alteration of the encoded protein. Of these, 8 are previously reported as pathogenic in either the germline state for GEI (dominant) or as oncogenic mutations.
117	
118	There are no established criteria for pathogenicity of mosaic variants, and here a scoring system specific to GEI was developed to address this. The strategy considered the impact of the variant on the encoded protein, published experimental data for the variant, known mechanisms for germline GEI in the gene with the variant, expression of the variant in relevant immune cells, as well as in silico prediction and population data. Understanding known germline mechanisms of disease associated with a gene aids in variant interpretation, since mosaic variants are likely to be heterozygous or hemizygous. As such, we would predict that disease-causing pathogenic mosaic variants will occur when a known corresponding germline equivalent is dominant, for example GOF, loss of regulatory function, dominant-negative, or haploinsufficiency mechanisms. Another important consideration for our scoring criteria is the tissue restriction of the variant. If a mosaic variant is limited to tissues that do not express the transcript/protein, it is unlikely to be pathogenic. Alternatively, for some mosaic GEI (e.g., VEXAS syndrome, ALPS-sFAS) variants are enriched in a subset of immune cells, and this enrichment or tissue restriction can help to identify pathogenicity of new variants.
119	
120	There are limitations to this scoring strategy. First, it is possible that mosaic variants lead to a ‘second-hit’ and cause disease when combined with a germline variant. Thus, analysis of germline variants, including structural variants, in the same gene is important. The high-depth sequencing approach used here is unable to determine whether mosaic variants in the same patient occur in the same cells, although we did not identify any pathogenic germline variants in the same gene in samples with mosaic variants. Second, the scoring strategy does not consider the VAF of a variant. This decision was made because the threshold at which a particular mosaic variant can cause disease is unknown and is likely highly dependent on the cell type expressing the variant and the gene product itself. In addition, it will require more experience with deep sequencing to actually detect low VAF variants with certainty to know if they can be associated with disease. For example, mosaic variants such as those in NLRP3 can be pathogenic at VAFs as low as 1.3%.^20 Third, there are likely additional mosaic-only GEI that do not have a germline equivalent, similar to VEXAS, and variants in these new genes will be difficult to score, emphasizing the need for rigorous functional testing to establish pathogenicity. Similarly, the STAT3 p.Ser614Arg variant detected in 2 patients here (known and undiagnosed) has been identified as mosaic in hypereosinophilic syndrome (in addition to cancers), but this disorder is not currently classified as a mosaic GEI. Therefore, scoring of this STAT3 variant led to a prediction of LMP rather than MP, also highlighting the intentionally conservative nature of this scoring system. Finally, the scoring system assumes that for genes with 2 copies, both alleles are equally expressed. However, monoallelic expression of genes on autosomes and skewed x-inactivation for heterozygous variants in females are both mechanisms whereby a single variant can cause disease.^10, 57, 58 Ultimately, these scoring criteria are not designed to diagnose patients with mosaic GEI, but to assist with the classification and prioritization of mosaic variants.
121	
122	Using this scoring system for mosaic pathogenicity, pathogenic or likely pathogenic mosaic variants were only identified in patients, with the majority being of uncertain mosaic significance (UMS). Of note, the 4 variants classified as “mosaic pathogenic” were in FAS and met the criteria for MP because we demonstrated enrichment in DNTs, highlighting the need for functional and/or cell-expression data to meet this score. Another 12 variants were classified as “likely mosaic pathogenic”, including 3 variants that are disease-causing for germline GEI and 4 that are reported as oncogenic. While of great interest, additional functional testing of these LMP variants will be required to determine disease causality for mosaic GEI. All variants in healthy patients were “likely mosaic benign” (2/12) or “uncertain mosaic significance” (10/12). These findings suggest that pathogenic and likely pathogenic mosaic variants in relevant genes of the immune system may be enriched in patients with undiagnosed immune dysregulation.
123	
124	Immune cell subsets were tested for enrichment of mosaic variants in FAS, TNFAIP3, NRAS, and UBA1, in patients with autoinflammatory and lymphoproliferative phenotypes, with the 4 FAS variants confirmed as pathogenic based on expression in DNTs. In the past, molecular diagnosis of ALPS-sFAS required purification of DNTs followed by targeted Sanger-based sequencing, supported by phenotyping DNTs and serum biomarkers.^13, 59
125	12 López-Nevado et al successfully used a gene-targeted NGS approach to identify mosaic FAS variants from whole blood DNA.^60 Here we demonstrate the utility of testing for mosaicism in multiple genes, which is particularly relevant for patients suspected of having ALPS as there is frequently phenotypic overlap with other disorders.
126	
127	While enrichment testing was not diagnostic for the other patients, of note there were three patients with predicted LOF (nonsense and frameshift) variants in TNFAIP3, all with lymphoproliferation. LOF variants in TNFAIP3 cause haploinsufficiency of A20 and immune dysregulation in the germline state, and B cell lymphomas and other malignancies in the somatic state.^53 In testing of two patients, there was enrichment of the variant in T cells in one and NK cells in the other, but the function of these variant-expressing cells is unknown. Two patients with a similar clinical phenotype of T cell EBV were identified as having mosaic missense variants in NRAS, with enrichment of the NRAS variant in the one patient tested here. The identification of mosaic variants in the same gene in patients with a similar clinical phenotype is suggestive of causality, but for TNFAIP3, NRAS and other variants of interest here, further functional studies are necessary to establish disease-causality. As the field of mosaic GEI continues to expand, developing efficient methods, likely using single cell techniques, to screen for the functional consequences of mosaic variants will be important for ascribing causality.
128	
129	As the field of mosaic GEI progresses, it will also be important to evaluate genetic mosaicism in tissue resident immune cells and other cell types at sites of immune development (e.g., thymus or bone marrow) or disease (e.g., skin, intestinal tract). Assessing different tissue compartments in patients can provide additional insight into both the developmental origins of somatic variants and their potential impact on the clinical phenotype. For example, intestinal epithelial cells have some of the highest rates of mosaic mutations, and individuals with inflammatory bowel disease show a further increased mutation rate.^61, 62 Efforts such as the Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues (SMaHT) initiative are working to better understand the prevalence and role of somatic variants in different human tissues in both health and disease.
130	
131	The baseline rate of mosaicism in genes relevant to the immune response is poorly understood,^63 but hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), responsible for generating immune cells, accumulate mutations over time.^64, 65 Perhaps not surprisingly, mosaic variants were also identified in currently healthy individuals, including young children and adults, although most do not alter the structure of the encoded protein. The individuals tested here were healthy at the time of sample collection, and future studies to assess whether the presence of mosaicism of the immune system is stable over time, portends disease, or accumulates with age will be important to understand how these genetic changes might alter the immune response. Of diagnostic relevance, clinicians should proceed with caution if and when deep sequencing clinical testing identifies a mosaic variant, since they can also be seen in healthy patients, demonstrating that most mosaic variants are not disease-causing.
132	
133	The major advantage of our approach is the ability to generate high-depth sequencing to accurately identify variants with a low VAF not detectable by standard-depth exome or genome sequencing. However, a limitation is that this approach will miss causative variants in genes that are not targeted. An alternative approach is to use existing exome data to identify mosaic variants. Of note, 50.8% (230/452) of the affected patients in the cohort here were also assessed for mosaicism by Ghosh et al. (accompanying manuscript) using exome sequencing. Most mosaic variants (22/27) identified in these samples using deep sequencing were not detected by exome sequencing while 5 variants with VAFs >5% were detected by both methods. However, exome reanalysis identified potentially pathogenic variants in multiple genes not covered by the deep sequencing panel including ITGB2, KIT, TSC2, BRCA1, and FOXI3 in their patient cohort. Thus, there are benefits and limitations to both methods.
134	
135	Other alternatives to discovery of mosaic variants include high-depth genome or exome or single-cell genome sequencing, although cost of this may be challenging in large patient cohorts.^18 These methods are also susceptible to sequencing errors that can distort results, and, in single-cell genome sequencing, allelic dropout can lead to mosaic variants not being sequenced.^66 Error-corrected sequencing can minimize sequencing errors, although it is currently more costly than a targeted deep sequencing panel in which vastly increased sequencing depth can partially compensate for sequencing errors.^67 Therefore, establishing a sequencing platform to screen individuals for potentially pathogenic mosaic variants in a clinically diverse patient population will require careful decision on priorities regarding limit of detection, discovery capacity, and cost. As new sequencing methods continue to emerge, our ability to detect mosaic variants at lower frequencies in a cost effective way will continue to improve.^10
136	
137	In summary, our deep sequencing pipeline identified mosaic variants in patients with immune dysregulation and healthy individuals. We proposed and tested criteria for assessing potential pathogenicity of mosaic variants in the context of GEI and demonstrate pathogenic and likely pathogenic mosaic variants in patients but not healthy individuals here. Further studies will be critical to establish disease-causality for these and other mosaic genetic changes affecting genes of the immune response. Overall, these results highlight the plasticity of genes encoding our immune system, and the need to better understand heterogeneity in health and disease states.
